lesson.title: One Chromosome Too Many, One Too Few
lesson.summary: Aneuploidy is having an abnormal number of copies of a particular chromosome, usually one too many, called trisomy, or one too few, called monosomy, and it is one of the most common outcomes of nondisjunction during meiosis.
lesson.body:
Aneuploidy means a cell's chromosome count deviates from the normal, complete set by whole chromosomes, most often just one chromosome, rather than by multiplying the entire chromosome set as happens in polyploidy. The two basic forms are trisomy, having three copies of a particular chromosome instead of the normal two, and monosomy, having only one copy instead of two. As the previous chapter explained, both arise from nondisjunction during meiosis, when a chromosome pair or a pair of sister chromatids fails to separate and produces a gamete with either an extra or a missing chromosome.

The best known example of trisomy in humans is Down syndrome, caused by trisomy 21, three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two. Individuals with Down syndrome have distinctive physical features, developmental delays, and an increased risk of certain heart defects, and the risk of a pregnancy affected by trisomy 21 rises with maternal age, because eggs remain arrested partway through meiosis I for decades and the machinery that holds homologous chromosomes together can degrade over that time. Chromosome 21 is one of the smallest human chromosomes, and this matters more than it might seem.

Trisomies of larger chromosomes are almost never seen in living newborns because they are usually lethal very early in development and end in miscarriage. Trisomy 18, Edwards syndrome, and trisomy 13, Patau syndrome, do sometimes result in live birth but involve severe medical complications and, on average, very short life expectancy. The pattern across all of these conditions is that smaller chromosomes carry fewer genes, so having a third copy throws off the dosage of fewer genes and is more survivable, which is exactly the gene dosage principle introduced in the chromosomal abnormalities chapter.

Monosomy of an autosome, a missing copy of any of chromosomes 1 through 22, is essentially never observed in a live birth, because losing an entire copy of dozens or hundreds of genes at once is even more disruptive to development than gaining one. The major exception involves the sex chromosomes. Turner syndrome results from monosomy of the X chromosome, a person with only a single X chromosome and no second sex chromosome, and unlike autosomal monosomies, this is compatible with life, producing a female with a specific set of developmental features including short stature and infertility. On the trisomy side of the sex chromosomes, Klinefelter syndrome results from an extra X chromosome in a male, producing an XXY karyotype. That the sex chromosomes tolerate an abnormal copy number so much better than the autosomes do reflects the fact that one X chromosome in every cell is normally inactivated anyway, which cushions the impact of gaining or losing one.
